rv.q: Rickson's galvanic new production of Mojo is guaranteed full houses.
It is the combination of strong plotting and zinging dialogue that makes this play so addictive and disconcerting.
You won't find much better ensemble acting than this, nor a play that so effectively punctures the pretensions of a hermetic gangland culture.
The trouble is, it all feels like a stylistic exercise: though Butterworth riffs intriguingly, Mojo is a thinly plotted piece without much heart.

Mojo was thrown on in a bravura piece of Royal Court programming under Stephen Daldry , and you can now see clearly where Jerusalem comes from in the groundswell of tragic destiny, the cultural tectonic shifts that define the action; the play has the sting of originality and the power of voodoo.
For all its initially impressive energy, the revival feels dated, its lack of chilling terror creating an evening of strikingly little substance.
There is not a false note among them and if Whishaw and Coyle command the centre stage, there are equally vivid contributions from Mays, Morgan and Grint as variously jittery sidekicks.

The ever-compelling Daniel Mays, with the look of a permanently surprised toilet brush and a Chaplinesque physicality, is in danger of acting everyone else off the stage as numpty tough Potts. The twist mid-way through the second act remains a good surprise as the rivals vie for supremacy.
But ultimately the play's barrage of gags undercuts its power as drama - the final revelation of responsibility and guilt doesn't seem to matter much.

cn.t: Butterworth's stylish 1995 gangland debut still packs punch in this star-studded revival, though some critics find it feels slighter compared to his later triumph Jerusalem. Brilliant performances elevate the Tarantino-esque dark comedy.
